paras.en: [[21:23|This saying therefore went abroad among the brethren, that that disciple should not die|Exivit ergo sermo iste inter fratres, quod discipulus ille non moritur]]. These are the words of the Evangelist relating how the disciples then present understood the words of Christ. For they thought Jesus signified that John would not die; and because they erred in this, John excludes this sense. [[21:23|And Jesus did not say to him: He should not die|Et non dixit Jesus, quia non moritur]], that is, by His words He did not signify that John would not die. [[21:23|but: So I will have him to remain till I come|Sed dixit : Sic eum volo manere donec veniam]] (in the sense touched on above), [[21:23|what is it to thee|quid ad te]]? For these were the words of Christ which have just been expounded. Now it is read in the life of blessed John the Evangelist that, when his death was at hand, the Lord Jesus came to him with the Apostles, inviting him to the most happy banquet of the elect in the fatherland. Therefore Christ said: So I will have him to remain till I come.

paras.t: Hic de quo Christus ista disseruit, est discipulus ille qui testimonium perhibet de his quæ in isto capitulo, seu in toto volumine isto, contenta sunt. Perhibuit autem Joannes testimonium de his quæ ad evangelicam pertinent legem, prædicando, docendo, miracula faciendo, irreprehensibiliter conversando, alios quoque magnos suos discipulos ad prædicandum mittendo, videlicet S. Ignatium, B. Polycarpum, etc. Unde in Apocalypsi asserit de se ipso : Qui testimonium perhibuit verbo Dei et testimonium Jesu Christi, quæcumque vidit. Et scripsit hæc, post reditum ab insula Patmos. Et scimus quia verum est testimonium ejus. Loquitur S. Joannes de se ipso in tertia persona quasi de alio; et quod ait, Scimus, etc., loquitur in persona sui omniumque perfectorum fidelium. Denique Joannes scripsit quæ audivit et vidit propriis sensibus immediate a Christo, saltem pro maxima parte; cetera audivit a fide dignis. Imo omnia scripsit inspirante ac dirigente Spiritu Sancto. Propter quod ait circa exordium primæ suæ epistolæ : Quod audivimus et vidimus, annuntiamus vobis. Ideo testimonium ejus certum idoneumque consistit, quoniam visa et audita certissime recitantur.
paras.en: [[21:24|This is that disciple who giveth testimony of these things|Hic est discipulus ille qui testimonium perhibet de his]]: he of whom Christ discoursed these things is the disciple who gives testimony of the things contained in this chapter, or in this whole volume. John gave testimony of the things that belong to the Gospel law by preaching, teaching, working miracles, living blamelessly, and also by sending other great disciples of his to preach, namely St Ignatius, blessed Polycarp, etc. Hence in the Apocalypse he asserts of himself: [[Apoc 1:2|Who hath given testimony to the word of God and the testimony of Jesus Christ, what things soever he hath seen|Qui testimonium perhibuit verbo Dei et testimonium Jesu Christi, quæcumque vidit]]. [[21:24|and hath written these things|Et scripsit hæc]], after his return from the island of Patmos. [[21:24|and we know that his testimony is true|Et scimus quia verum est testimonium ejus]]. St John speaks of himself in the third person as of another; and in saying, We know, etc., he speaks in the person of himself and of all the perfect faithful. Further, John wrote what he heard and saw with his own senses directly from Christ, at least for the greatest part; the rest he heard from trustworthy men. Nay, he wrote all by the inspiration and direction of the Holy Ghost. Hence he says near the beginning of his first epistle: [[1 John 1:1|That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen|Quod audivimus et vidimus]], [[1 John 1:2|and declare unto you|annuntiamus vobis]]. Therefore his testimony stands certain and fit, since things seen and heard are related most surely.

paras.t: Sunt autem, hoc est fuerunt, et alia multa quæ fecit Jesus, id est signa et opera omni memoria ac descriptione dignissima, quæ Jesus a principio incarnationis et nativitatis fecit per se et per suos usque ad ea quæ hic dicuntur, vel usque ad missionem Paracleti. Quæ si scribantur per singula, hoc est sigillatim, particulariter et seorsum, nec ipsum arbitror mundum capere posse eos qui scribendi sunt libros, si omnia illa taliter describerentur per singula : hoc est, omnium hominum in mundo hoc inferiori viventium capacitatem transcenderent. Si autem intelligatur de mundo et captione, quantum ad spatium loci, videlicet, quod mundus continere non posset tot libros, tunc accipienda sunt verba ista per hyperbolen seu excessum. Interdum enim homo aliqua dicit per excessum, ad designandum magnitudinem rei quæ recitatur : ut dum in libro Judicum scribitur, quod filii Benjamin sic ad certum jactabant funda lapidem, quod capillum tangere potuerunt. Itemque in Genesi Pharao ad Joseph : Absque tui, inquit, oris imperio, nemo movebit manum aut pedem in tota terra Ægypti. Talia autem sine mendacio asseruntur, quoniam narrans agnoscit quousque credatur, nec intendit decipere, sed veritatem ipsam evidentius reserare : quod fieri nequit, nisi per sermonem figuralem et hyperbolicum. Porro, quoniam Christus erat Deus et homo, virtus omnipotens et sapientia increata operans per humanitatem assumptam, sicut per instrumentum conjunctum, animatum ac proprium, elucescit quod documenta et opera ejus excellentissima erant.
paras.en: [[21:25|But there are|Sunt autem]], that is, there were, [[21:25|also many other things which Jesus did|et alia multa quæ fecit Jesus]], that is, signs and works most worthy of all remembrance and record, which Jesus did from the beginning of His incarnation and birth, by Himself and by His own, up to the things here told, or up to the sending of the Paraclete. [[21:25|which, if they were written every one|Quæ si scribantur per singula]], that is, one by one, in particular and separately, [[21:25|the world itself. I think, would not be able to contain the books that should be written|nec ipsum arbitror mundum capere posse eos qui scribendi sunt libros]], if all those things were so described one by one: that is, they would surpass the capacity of all men living in this lower world [Denis takes *capere*, “contain”, first in the sense of “grasp”]. But if it be understood of the world and of containing as to extent of space, namely that the world could not hold so many books, then these words are to be taken as hyperbole or excess. For sometimes one says things by excess to signify the greatness of the thing related: as when it is written in the book of Judges that the sons of Benjamin slung stones so accurately that they could hit a hair[[Judg 20:16||]]. And in Genesis Pharao to Joseph: [[Gen 41:44|without thy commandment no man shall move hand or foot in all the land of Egypt|Absque tui … oris imperio … terra Ægypti]]. Such things are asserted without lying, since the narrator knows how far he will be believed, and does not mean to deceive, but to disclose the truth itself more clearly, which cannot be done except by figurative and hyperbolic speech. Further, since Christ was God and man, the almighty power and uncreated wisdom[[1 Cor 1:24||]] working through the assumed humanity as through a conjoined, living and proper instrument, it shines forth that His teachings and works were most excellent.
